title: Colour from a vat: understanding plant-derived indigo
deck: Indigo dyeing is a sequence of plant knowledge, chemistry and patient handwork; institutional records also show why colourfastness and cultural specificity need careful language.

sections.heading: Blue appears through process
sections.text: Indigo is associated with plants, yet the blue on cloth is the result of preparation and controlled chemistry rather than direct rubbing of a blue petal. Dyeing makes a soluble form available before oxidation develops colour.

sections.heading: Pattern, reserve and the working vat
sections.text: Smithsonian teaching material documents batik and botanical dye practice among named Miao and Dong makers in Guizhou. Wax-resist patterning and vat dyeing are related steps, each demanding control of material and timing.

sections.heading: Several plants, not one universal recipe
sections.text: Different regions have obtained indigo precursors from different botanical sources. Kew’s account separates the chemical colourant from a single species story, while the Smithsonian example stays tied to documented makers.

sections.heading: Colourfast is always qualified
sections.text: Conservation research shows that natural dyes vary in resistance to light and washing. Mordants, fibre type, concentration and later exposure can change performance, so natural is not a technical synonym for permanent.

sections.heading: Technique carries cultural knowledge
sections.text: A dye vat is both a chemical system and part of a learned practice. Institutional documentation can describe materials and visible steps, but it cannot replace the language, experience and authority of sustaining communities.

sections.heading: What the evidence does not establish
sections.text: These sources do not support universal sustainability claims for natural dyes or the idea that one recipe represents all indigo traditions. Crop production, water use, mordants and workshop conditions require case-specific evidence.
